claim: Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens suppress human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) replication, restore immune function, and prevent the development of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) in individuals who are able to adhere to therapy.
source: In individuals who are able to adhere to combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), therapy suppresses human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) replication, restores immune function, and prevents the development of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) (Deeks et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deeks et al., 2013

claim: More than 20 different antiretroviral drugs belonging to six main classes are currently approved for clinical use.
source: More than 20 different antiretroviral drugs belonging to six main classes are currently approved for clinical use (Pau and George, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pau and George, 2014

claim: Antiretroviral drugs block different steps of the HIV replication cycle, such as reverse transcription, proviral integration, or virus particle maturation, depending on the class.
source: Depending on the class, these drugs block different steps of the HIV replication cycle, such as reverse transcription, proviral integration, or virus particle maturation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of antiretroviral drug mechanisms

claim: Current ART regimens typically consist of two nucleotide or nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and a third drug of another class.
source: Current ART regimens typically consist of two nucleotide or nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and a third drug of another class, for example, a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI), a protease inhibitor (PI), or an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI).
evidence: Based on established clinical practice and knowledge

claim: ART is not curative and has to be sustained lifelong despite efficient suppression of HIV replication.
source: Despite the efficient suppression of HIV replication, ART is not curative and has to be sustained lifelong.
evidence: Based on established scientific consensus

claim: Persistence of viral reservoirs forms the major obstacle to an HIV cure.
source: Persistence of viral reservoirs forms the major obstacle to an HIV cure (Deeks et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deeks et al., 2016

claim: Viral reservoir markers, such as low-level HIV RNA in plasma (residual viremia) and cell-associated (CA) HIV DNA and RNA, can be measured in most treated individuals with plasma HIV RNA suppressed to below the limit of quantification of commercial assays.
source: Viral reservoir markers, such as low-level HIV RNA in plasma (residual viremia) and cell-associated (CA) HIV DNA and RNA, can be measured in most treated individuals with plasma HIV RNA suppressed to below the limit of quantification of commercial assays (Jacobs et al., 2019; Pasternak and Berkhout, 2018; Pasternak et al., 2013; Avettand-Fènoël et al., 2016; Sharaf and Li, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: HIV latent reservoirs persist primarily by cell longevity and proliferation.
source: Although HIV latent reservoirs persist primarily by cell longevity and proliferation (Chomont et al., 2009; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2014), replenishment of the reservoirs by residual virus replication despite ART has been proposed as an alternative mechanism of HIV persistence (Chun et al., 2005; Lorenzo-Redondo et al., 2016; Sigal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chomont et al., 2009; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2014

claim: Replenishment of the reservoirs by residual virus replication despite ART has been proposed as an alternative mechanism of HIV persistence.
source: Although HIV latent reservoirs persist primarily by cell longevity and proliferation (Chomont et al., 2009; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2014), replenishment of the reservoirs by residual virus replication despite ART has been proposed as an alternative mechanism of HIV persistence (Chun et al., 2005; Lorenzo-Redondo et al., 2016; Sigal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chun et al., 2005; Lorenzo-Redondo et al., 2016; Sigal et al., 2011

claim: The possibility of residual virus replication despite ART remains a matter of longstanding debate in HIV research field.
source: The latter possibility remains a matter of longstanding debate in HIV research field (Martinez-Picado and Deeks, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martinez-Picado and Deeks, 2016

claim: Residual HIV replication can result from insufficient penetration of antiretroviral drugs into tissues and anatomic sanctuaries, causing reduced local drug concentrations in tissue sites.
source: Residual HIV replication can result from insufficient penetration of antiretroviral drugs into tissues and anatomic sanctuaries, causing reduced local drug concentrations in tissue sites (Estes et al., 2017; Fletcher et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Estes et al., 2017; Fletcher et al., 2014

claim: Most (but not all) studies could not demonstrate any measurable virus evolution in peripheral blood and tissues of ART-treated individuals.
source: However, most (but not all) studies could not demonstrate any measurable virus evolution in peripheral blood and tissues of ART-treated individuals (Bozzi et al., 2019; Van Zyl et al., 2017; Joos et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bozzi et al., 2019; Van Zyl et al., 2017; Joos et al., 2008

claim: The lack of significant virus evolution on ART is considered one of the strongest arguments against residual HIV replication.
source: This lack of significant virus evolution on ART is considered one of the strongest arguments against residual HIV replication.
evidence: Based on inference from the scientific literature

claim: A transient increase in episomal HIV DNA has been demonstrated in a number of trials of ART intensification with raltegravir, an INSTI.
source: On the other hand, a transient increase in episomal HIV DNA has been demonstrated in a number of trials of ART intensification with raltegravir, an INSTI (Buzón et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buzón et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2013a

claim: The accumulation of unintegrated HIV DNA observed upon blocking integration revealed ongoing integration events prior to intensification.
source: This accumulation of unintegrated HIV DNA, observed upon blocking integration, revealed ongoing integration events prior to intensification.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental observation

claim: Because all other antiretroviral drug classes act upstream of INSTIs, ongoing integration events imply that complete rounds of HIV replication (infection of new cells) had been ongoing pre-intensification.
source: Because all other antiretroviral drug classes act upstream of INSTIs, this implies that complete rounds of HIV replication (infection of new cells) had been ongoing pre-intensification.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the mechanism of action of antiretroviral drugs

claim: No decrease in residual HIV viremia could be demonstrated in intensification trials.
source: However, no decrease in residual HIV viremia could be demonstrated in these and other intensification trials (Gandhi et al., 2010; McMahon et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gandhi et al., 2010; McMahon et al., 2010; Hatano et al., 2011

claim: All current antiretroviral drugs act by preventing the infection of new cells and are not expected to inhibit HIV RNA transcription or virus production in the long-lived reservoir cells that were infected prior to ART initiation, or in the progeny of such cells.
source: All current antiretroviral drugs act by preventing the infection of new cells and are not expected to inhibit HIV RNA transcription or virus production in the long-lived reservoir cells that were infected prior to ART initiation, or in the progeny of such cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of antiretroviral drug mechanisms

claim: If regimens are equally potent in stopping the infection of new cells, one would not expect to detect a difference in residual viremia or CA RNA levels between ART regimens.
source: Therefore, if regimens are equally potent in stopping the infection of new cells, one would not expect to detect a difference in residual viremia or CA RNA levels between ART regimens.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the mechanism of action of antiretroviral drugs

claim: Finding a difference in residual viremia or CA RNA levels between ART regimens would suggest that some regimens are more potent in suppressing residual replication than others.
source: Consequently, finding such a difference would suggest that some regimens are more potent in suppressing residual replication than others, arguing that virus suppression is less complete with at least some of the regimens.
evidence: Based on logical inference

claim: A number of studies reported lower levels of residual viremia in individuals treated with NNRTI-based, compared to PI-based, ART regimens.
source: A number of studies reported lower levels of residual viremia in individuals treated with NNRTI-based, compared to PI-based, ART regimens (Geretti et al., 2019; Darcis et al., 2020a, reviewed in Darcis et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geretti et al., 2019; Darcis et al., 2020a; Darcis et al., 2020b

claim: Few studies have compared levels of CA HIV reservoir markers between different ART regimens.
source: However, to date, few studies have compared levels of CA HIV reservoir markers between different ART regimens (Nicastri et al., 2008; Sarmati et al., 2012; Kiselinova et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nicastri et al., 2008; Sarmati et al., 2012; Kiselinova et al., 2015

claim: CA HIV unspliced RNA and total HIV DNA were quantified in two cohorts (n = 100, n = 124) of individuals treated with triple ART regimens consisting of two NRTIs plus either an NNRTI or a PI.
source: CA HIV unspliced RNA and total HIV DNA were quantified in two cohorts (n = 100, n = 124) of individuals treated with triple ART regimens consisting of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus either an NNRTI or a PI.
evidence: Describes the experimental design and measurements performed in the study

claim: In both cohorts, levels of CA HIV RNA and DNA strongly correlated (rho = 0.70 and rho = 0.54).
source: In both cohorts, levels of CA HIV RNA and DNA strongly correlated (rho = 0.70 and rho = 0.54) and both markers were lower in NNRTI-treated than in PI-treated individuals.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from both cohorts

claim: Both CA HIV RNA and DNA markers were lower in NNRTI-treated than in PI-treated individuals in both cohorts.
source: In both cohorts, levels of CA HIV RNA and DNA strongly correlated (rho = 0.70 and rho = 0.54) and both markers were lower in NNRTI-treated than in PI-treated individuals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both cohorts

claim: In the multivariable analysis, CA RNA in both cohorts remained significantly reduced in NNRTI-treated individuals (padj = 0.02 in both cohorts).
source: In the multivariable analysis, CA RNA in both cohorts remained significantly reduced in NNRTI-treated individuals (padj = 0.02 in both cohorts), with a similar but weaker association between the ART regimen and total HIV DNA (padj = 0.048 and padj = 0.10).
evidence: Supported by multivariable statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The association between the ART regimen and total HIV DNA was similar but weaker than for CA RNA (padj = 0.048 and padj = 0.10).
source: In the multivariable analysis, CA RNA in both cohorts remained significantly reduced in NNRTI-treated individuals (padj = 0.02 in both cohorts), with a similar but weaker association between the ART regimen and total HIV DNA (padj = 0.048 and padj = 0.10).
evidence: Supported by multivariable statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: No differences in CA HIV RNA or DNA levels were observed between individual NNRTIs or individual PIs.
source: No differences in CA HIV RNA or DNA levels were observed between individual NNRTIs or individual PIs, but CA HIV RNA was lower in individuals treated with either nevirapine or efavirenz, compared to PI-treated individuals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing individual drugs

claim: CA HIV RNA was lower in individuals treated with either nevirapine or efavirenz, compared to PI-treated individuals.
source: No differences in CA HIV RNA or DNA levels were observed between individual NNRTIs or individual PIs, but CA HIV RNA was lower in individuals treated with either nevirapine or efavirenz, compared to PI-treated individuals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing specific drugs

claim: These differences in CA HIV RNA and DNA levels by treatment regimen suggest that NNRTIs are more potent in suppressing HIV residual replication than PIs.
source: Therefore, these differences in CA HIV RNA and DNA levels by treatment regimen suggest that NNRTIs are more potent in suppressing HIV residual replication than PIs, which may result in a smaller viral reservoir size.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing differences between regimens

claim: More potent suppression of HIV residual replication by NNRTIs may result in a smaller viral reservoir size.
source: Therefore, these differences in CA HIV RNA and DNA levels by treatment regimen suggest that NNRTIs are more potent in suppressing HIV residual replication than PIs, which may result in a smaller viral reservoir size.
evidence: Speculative inference from the experimental data

claim: Participants for the COBRA cohort were recruited at two clinical sites in Amsterdam (The Netherlands) and London (UK).
source: Participants for the COmorBidity in Relation to AIDS (COBRA) cohort were recruited at two clinical sites in Amsterdam (The Netherlands) and London (UK) from ongoing prospective cohort studies on co-morbidity and aging in HIV, the AGEhIV Cohort Study in Amsterdam (Schouten et al., 2014), and the POPPY study in London (De Francesco et al., 2016).
evidence: Describes the study design and participant recruitment

claim: All COBRA participants were required to be at least 45 years of age.
source: All participants were required to be at least 45 years of age.
evidence: Describes the inclusion criteria for the study

claim: For the COBRA study, only peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples from the first study visit were used: 63 participants out of 100 were from the Amsterdam sub-cohort and 37 were from the London sub-cohort.
source: Although most COBRA participants had two study visits within 2 years, for the present cross-sectional study, only peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples from the first study visit were used: 63 participants out of 100 were from the Amsterdam sub-cohort and 37 were from the London sub-cohort.
evidence: Describes the study design and sample selection

claim: In the COBRA cohort, 95% were male and the median age was 55 years (interquartile range, 51–61 years).
source: In brief, 95% were male and the median age was 55 years (interquartile range, 51–61 years).
evidence: Describes demographic characteristics of the study participants

claim: In the COBRA cohort, 98 participants had undetectable plasma HIV RNA (<50 copies/ml) and two had detectable but low levels (66 and 90 copies/ml).
source: 98 participants had undetectable plasma HIV RNA (<50 copies/ml) and two had detectable but low levels (66 and 90 copies/ml).
evidence: Describes virological characteristics of the study participants

claim: COBRA participants had a median of 118 (62–163) months of cumulative and 99 (47–146) months of continuous virological suppression on ART prior to the measurements.
source: Participants had a median of 118 (62–163) months of cumulative and 99 (47–146) months of continuous virological suppression on ART prior to the measurements and had been treated with their current NNRTI or PI regimen for a median of 69 (38–116) months.
evidence: Describes treatment history of the study participants

claim: COBRA participants had been treated with their current NNRTI or PI regimen for a median of 69 (38–116) months.
source: Participants had a median of 118 (62–163) months of cumulative and 99 (47–146) months of continuous virological suppression on ART prior to the measurements and had been treated with their current NNRTI or PI regimen for a median of 69 (38–116) months.
evidence: Describes treatment history of the study participants

claim: In the COBRA cohort, the duration of virological suppression on ART and the duration of current regimen prior to the measurements were significantly different between NNRTI- and PI-treated participants.
source: The duration of virological suppression on ART and the duration of current regimen prior to the measurements were significantly different between NNRTI- and PI-treated participants (cumulative suppression: median of 137 vs 90 months, respectively, p = 0.004; continuous suppression, median of 118 vs 62 months, respectively, p = 0.001; current regimen: median of 99 vs 48 months, respectively, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of treatment duration data

claim: The median CA HIV RNA level in the COBRA cohort was 2.15 (1.58–2.52) log10 copies/μg total RNA.
source: The median CA HIV RNA and total HIV DNA levels in the COBRA cohort were 2.15 (1.58–2.52) log10 copies/μg total RNA and 2.50 (1.84–2.77) log10 copies/106 PBMC, respectively.
evidence: Describes experimental measurements in the COBRA cohort

claim: The median total HIV DNA level in the COBRA cohort was 2.50 (1.84–2.77) log10 copies/106 PBMC.
source: The median CA HIV RNA and total HIV DNA levels in the COBRA cohort were 2.15 (1.58–2.52) log10 copies/μg total RNA and 2.50 (1.84–2.77) log10 copies/106 PBMC, respectively.

claim: In the COBRA cohort, significant correlations with both HIV RNA and DNA were observed for the plasma HIV RNA zenith (rho = 0.22, p = 0.04 and rho = 0.36, p = 0.0004, respectively).
source: Significant correlations with both HIV RNA and DNA were observed for the plasma HIV RNA zenith (rho = 0.22, p = 0.04 and rho = 0.36, p = 0.0004, respectively), but not for any other variable.

claim: In the COBRA cohort, duration of cumulative virological suppression and duration of the current regimen were not associated with either CA HIV RNA or DNA.
source: Duration of cumulative virological suppression and duration of the current regimen were also not associated with either CA HIV RNA or DNA (cumulative suppression: rho = 0.04, p = 0.68 and rho = -0.06, p = 0.60; current regimen: rho = 0.02, p = 0.82 and rho = 0.02, p = 0.87).
